chapter.name: Permutations and Combinations
chapter.blurb: This chapter builds counting techniques that avoid listing: the fundamental principle of counting, factorial notation, and permutations of distinct objects with and without repetition, of objects that are not all distinct, and under restrictions. It then introduces combinations, where order is not important, with the formula for C(n, r), its properties, and their use in selecting committees, teams and cards.

scope_in.item: State and use the fundamental principle of counting (multiplication principle) for two, three or more events in succession, by filling vacant places one at a time

Count words, codes, signals, numbers and outcomes with repetition allowed or not allowed, filling the restricted place (e.g. the units place of an even number) first, and adding the counts of separate cases such as signals of 2, 3, 4 or 5 flags

Define a permutation as an arrangement in a definite order of objects taken some or all at a time, and use P(n, r) = n(n - 1)...(n - r + 1) for n different objects taken r at a time without repetition

Use factorial notation: n! = 1 x 2 x ... x n, 0! = 1, n! = n x (n - 1)!; evaluate and simplify expressions such as 7!/5!, 12!/(10! x 2!), n!/(r! x (n - r)!), and solve equations such as 1/8! + 1/9! = x/10!
Use P(n, r) = n!/(n - r)! for 0 <= r <= n, with P(n, n) = n! and P(n, 0) = 1, and the count n^r when repetition is allowed; solve simple equations in P(n, r) for n or r
Count the permutations of n objects that are not all distinct using n!/p! and n!/(p1! x p2! x ... x pk!): words with repeated letters, indistinguishable discs, numbers with repeated digits

Count permutations under restrictions: given objects all together (treated as one object) or not all together (total minus together), letters fixed at given places, numbers that may not begin with 0, objects kept apart by placing them in gaps, women in the even places, a fixed number of letters between two letters, and words listed in dictionary order
Define a combination as a selection in which order is not important; use P(n, r) = C(n, r) x r! and C(n, r) = n!/(r! x (n - r)!) for 0 <= r <= n, with C(n, 0) = C(n, n) = 1
Use the properties C(n, n - r) = C(n, r); C(n, a) = C(n, b) implies a = b or n = a + b; and C(n, r) + C(n, r - 1) = C(n + 1, r), including its proof; solve simple equations in C(n, r)

Count selections with C(n, r): handshakes, chords, committees and teams drawn from two or more groups, card selections from a pack of 52, compulsory items, and 'exactly', 'at least' and 'at most' conditions by adding cases
Combine selection and arrangement: choose letters with combinations and then arrange them (words of given numbers of vowels and consonants)

concepts.name: Fundamental principle of counting
concepts.description: The multiplication principle for events occurring in succession, applied by filling vacant places one at a time, with or without repetition, and adding the counts of separate cases.
concepts.idea: Instead of listing every possibility, count the ways each successive choice can be made and multiply them.
concepts.rule: If an event can occur in m different ways, following which another event can occur in n different ways, then the total number of occurrences of the events in the given order is m x n; the same holds for any finite number of events (m x n x p for three). Fill the most restricted place first, and add the counts of separate cases such as signals of 2, 3, 4 or 5 flags.
concepts.example: 3-digit numbers from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: 5 x 5 x 5 = 125 if repetition is allowed and 5 x 4 x 3 = 60 if it is not.

questions.q: The fundamental principle of counting states that if an event can occur in m different ways, following which another event can occur in n different ways, then the total number of occurrences of the events in the given order is

questions.q: The fundamental principle of counting is also known as the
questions.a: multiplication principle

o: If one event can occur in m ways and, following it, another can occur in n ways, then the two together can occur in m + n ways
It can be generalised to any finite number of events
For three successive events that can occur in m, n and p ways, the total is m x n x p
It is also known as the multiplication principle

questions.a: The units place is the restricted place: it must be 2 or 4, so it can be filled in 2 ways, and it is filled first for that reason. The tens place can then be filled by any of the 5 digits, because repetition is allowed. By the multiplication principle the number of such numbers is 2 x 5 = 10.

questions.q: How many 4-digit even numbers with no digit repeated can be formed from the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5? (A 4-digit number cannot begin with 0.) Explain why two cases are needed.
questions.a: The units digit must be 0, 2 or 4, but whether 0 has been used changes the choices for the thousands place, so two cases are needed. Case 1, units digit 0: the thousands, hundreds and tens places can be filled in 5 x 4 x 3 = 60 ways. Case 2, units digit 2 or 4 (2 ways): the thousands place cannot be 0 or the units digit, so 4 ways; then the hundreds place has 4 ways and the tens place 3 ways, giving 2 x 4 x 4 x 3 = 96. Total = 60 + 96 = 156.
s: Case units digit 0: 5 x 4 x 3 = 60
Case units digit 2 or 4: 2 x 4 x 4 x 3 = 96, with 0 excluded from the thousands place
Adds the cases to get 156 and explains that 0 in the units place changes the count for the thousands place

questions.q: A cafe offers 4 kinds of sandwich and 3 kinds of drink. Ravi says a meal of one sandwich and one drink can be chosen in 4 + 3 = 7 ways. Evaluate his claim.
questions.a: Ravi is wrong. For every one of the 4 sandwiches there are 3 possible drinks, so by the multiplication principle the number of meals is 4 x 3 = 12, not 7. Adding would count the ways of choosing just one item (a sandwich or a drink), not a pair.
s: Says the claim is wrong because each of the 4 sandwiches can go with each of the 3 drinks
Gives the correct count 4 x 3 = 12

questions.q: Create a counting problem about forming a 3-symbol code whose answer by the multiplication principle is 5 x 4 x 3 = 60. Then change one condition so that the answer becomes 5 x 5 x 5 = 125, and explain what the change does.
questions.a: Sample: 'How many 3-letter codes can be formed from the letters A, B, C, D, E if no letter may be repeated?' The first place can be filled in 5 ways, the second in 4 and the third in 3, so there are 5 x 4 x 3 = 60 codes. Changed version: 'How many 3-letter codes can be formed from A, B, C, D, E if letters may be repeated?' Now each of the 3 places can be filled in 5 ways, so there are 5 x 5 x 5 = 125 codes. Allowing repetition means a symbol already used is still available, so the number of choices does not drop from place to place.
s: States a valid problem with 5 symbols, 3 ordered places and no repetition, giving 5 x 4 x 3 = 60
States the changed problem with repetition allowed, giving 5 x 5 x 5 = 125
Explains that with repetition each place keeps all 5 choices, whereas without it the choices fall by one each time

concepts.name: Factorial notation
concepts.description: The meaning of n! as the product of the first n natural numbers, the convention 0! = 1, the relation n! = n x (n - 1)!, and the evaluation and simplification of expressions involving factorials.
concepts.idea: n! is shorthand for the product 1 x 2 x 3 x ... x n, which keeps turning up when arrangements are counted.
concepts.rule: n! = 1 x 2 x 3 x ... x (n - 1) x n, and 0! = 1 by definition. For a natural number n, n! = n x (n - 1)! = n x (n - 1) x (n - 2)! and so on, so a quotient of factorials is simplified by cancelling the smaller factorial, not by dividing the numbers.

questions.q: Find the natural number n for which (n + 2)! = 20 x n!.
questions.a: (n + 2)! = (n + 2)(n + 1) x n!, so the equation becomes (n + 2)(n + 1) x n! = 20 x n!. Dividing by n! (which is not zero): (n + 2)(n + 1) = 20, i.e. n^2 + 3n - 18 = 0, so (n + 6)(n - 3) = 0 and n = 3 or n = -6. As n is a natural number, n = 3. Check: 5! = 120 and 20 x 3! = 120.

s: Writes the equation 1/4! + 1/5! = x/6!
Expresses 5! and 6! in terms of 4! and solves to get x = 36

concepts.name: Permutations of distinct objects: P(n, r) and n^r
concepts.description: A permutation as an arrangement in a definite order; the number P(n, r) = n!/(n - r)! of permutations of n different objects taken r at a time without repetition, the count n^r when repetition is allowed, and simple equations in P(n, r).
concepts.idea: When order matters and the objects are all different, the number of arrangements of r of them is found by filling r places in succession.
concepts.rule: P(n, r) = n(n - 1)(n - 2)...(n - r + 1) = n!/(n - r)! for 0 <= r <= n, with P(n, n) = n! and P(n, 0) = 1. If repetition is allowed, the number of permutations of n different objects taken r at a time is n^r.
concepts.example: 3-letter words from the letters of NUMBER: P(6, 3) = 6 x 5 x 4 = 120 without repetition, and 6^3 = 216 with repetition.

concepts.name: Permutations when the objects are not all distinct
concepts.description: Counting the distinct arrangements of n objects of which some are alike, using n!/p! and n!/(p1! x p2! x ... x pk!), for words with repeated letters, indistinguishable discs and numbers with repeated digits.
concepts.idea: If some objects are alike, swapping the alike objects among themselves gives no new arrangement, so the n! arrangements of 'labelled' objects over-count.
concepts.rule: The number of permutations of n objects taken all at a time, where p1 objects are of one kind, p2 of a second kind, ..., pk of a kth kind and the rest, if any, are all different, is n!/(p1! x p2! x ... x pk!). With only one group of p alike objects this is n!/p!.
concepts.example: ROOT: 4!/2! = 12 arrangements. ALLAHABAD (4 As, 2 Ls): 9!/(4! x 2!) = 7560.

Justifies with 6!/(4! x 2!) = 15
Shows that a 3 + 3 split gives 6!/(3! x 3!) = 20, not 15

concepts.name: Permutations under restrictions
concepts.description: Arrangements subject to a condition: particular objects together or not all together, particular objects in fixed or specified places, numbers that may not begin with 0, objects kept apart by placing them in gaps, and words listed in dictionary order.
concepts.idea: A restriction is handled by dealing with the restricted objects or places first, or by counting everything and subtracting the unwanted arrangements.
concepts.rule: Objects that must stay together are treated temporarily as a single object, and the result is multiplied by the number of arrangements inside that object. 'Not all together' = total - 'all together'. Fix the objects whose places are given and arrange the rest. Numbers beginning with 0 are subtracted. To keep objects apart, arrange the others first and place the separated objects in the gaps. Dictionary rank is found by counting the words that begin with each earlier letter.
concepts.example: DAUGHTER with the 3 vowels together: 6! x 3! = 4320; with the vowels not all together: 8! - 4320 = 36000.

questions.a: Sample: 'In how many arrangements of all the letters of EQUATION, each used once, do all the vowels occur together?' EQUATION has 8 different letters: 5 vowels (E, U, A, I, O) and 3 consonants (Q, T, N). Treat the 5 vowels as a single object; with the 3 consonants this makes 4 objects, which can be arranged in 4! = 24 ways. Inside the single object the 5 vowels can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways. By the multiplication principle the answer is 4! x 5! = 2880. (Another valid question: vowels together and consonants together, 2! x 5! x 3! = 1440.)
s: Frames a clear question in which a named group of letters of EQUATION must stay together
Treats the group as a single object and counts the arrangements of the resulting objects
Multiplies by the arrangements within the group and reaches the correct total for the question framed (2880 for all vowels together)

concepts.name: Combinations: C(n, r) and its properties
concepts.description: A combination as a selection in which order is not important; the relation P(n, r) = C(n, r) x r!, the formula C(n, r) = n!/(r! x (n - r)!), and the properties C(n, 0) = C(n, n) = 1, C(n, r) = C(n, n - r), C(n, a) = C(n, b) implies a = b or n = a + b, and C(n, r) + C(n, r - 1) = C(n + 1, r).
concepts.idea: Each selection of r objects can be arranged in r! orders, so there are r! times as many permutations as combinations.
concepts.rule: P(n, r) = C(n, r) x r!, so C(n, r) = n!/(r! x (n - r)!) for 0 <= r <= n. C(n, 0) = C(n, n) = 1. C(n, n - r) = C(n, r): selecting r objects is the same as rejecting n - r. If C(n, a) = C(n, b) then a = b or n = a + b. C(n, r) + C(n, r - 1) = C(n + 1, r).
concepts.example: C(4, 2) = 4!/(2! x 2!) = 6: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD. If C(n, 9) = C(n, 8) then n = 17.

So the number of permutations is 10 x 2 = 20, which agrees with P(5, 2) = 5 x 4 = 20.
s: Lists the 10 combinations of 5 named objects taken 2 at a time

Confirms 10 x 2 = 20 = P(5, 2)

concepts.name: Counting selections with combinations
concepts.description: Using C(n, r) to count handshakes, chords, committees, teams, card selections and course programmes, including selections drawn from several groups (multiply), 'at least' and 'at most' conditions (add cases), compulsory items, and selections that are then arranged.
concepts.idea: When only who or what is chosen matters, count combinations; choices made from separate groups are multiplied, and alternative cases are added.
concepts.rule: A selection of r from n distinct things can be made in C(n, r) ways. Choosing a from one group AND b from another gives C(n1, a) x C(n2, b). 'At least' or 'at most' conditions are split into exact cases whose counts are added. Compulsory items are set aside first. If the chosen objects must then be arranged, multiply by the factorial of the number chosen.
concepts.example: A committee of 3 from 2 men and 3 women: C(5, 3) = 10 in all; with exactly 1 man and 2 women: C(2, 1) x C(3, 2) = 6.

questions.q: Frame a selection problem about choosing a team of 4 from 5 boys and 4 girls in which an 'at least' condition forces two separate cases to be added. List the cases and find the answer.
questions.a: Sample: 'A team of 4 is to be chosen from 5 boys and 4 girls. In how many ways can this be done if the team has at least 3 girls?' The cases are (a) 3 girls and 1 boy: C(4, 3) x C(5, 1) = 4 x 5 = 20; (b) 4 girls and no boy: C(4, 4) = 1. Since exactly one of the cases happens, the counts are added: 20 + 1 = 21.

Lists the two cases and counts each with a product of combinations
Adds the cases to reach the correct total for the problem framed (21 for at least 3 girls)
